title: Bhadda Kapilani
hook: Kassapa's wife parts from him at a crossroads, later becomes a nun, and is named foremost among the nuns in remembering past lives (AN 1.14; Therigatha)

segments.voice: Yesterday: sangiti, the reciting together Kassapa called so the teaching isn't lost. Today we go back to the woman who walked out of the house beside him, and follow her.

He takes the road to the right. She takes the road to the left. That's the whole parting, as the commentary tells it. Pippali and Bhadda, who married as friends and left home together, had been walking one behind the other in simple robes since they left their great house. At a crossroads they stop. People who see them pass might think they're still a couple, and that could cloud the life they've chosen. So at the fork they go separate ways. We followed him for most of a week. Today is about her.
screen: `TWO ROBES ON ONE ROAD.` → `A FORK AHEAD.` → `RIGHT FOR HIM, LEFT FOR HER.`

segments.voice: First, the parting. In the commentary it's done with respect, not regret. They've shared a house and a friendship; now each walks toward the same goal by a separate road. Second, the waiting. When Bhadda left, the commentary says, there was not yet an order of nuns. So she waited, and lived the homeless life as best she could. Later, when women were ordained, she was ordained among them, and in time she reached the goal. Third, her gift. In the list of foremost disciples, the Buddha names Bhadda Kapilani foremost among the nuns who remember past lives. Not because of her husband: in her own right, in her own line of the list. Fourth, her own verses. In the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, Bhadda begins by praising Kassapa: the Buddha's true heir, who knows his former lives and has reached the end. Then she turns and says the same of herself. She too has that knowledge; she too has come to the end. They both saw the misery of the world, she says, and went forth, and both are now freed, at peace. She doesn't make herself smaller to praise him, or him smaller to claim her place. She stands beside him in the poem the way she walked beside him out of the house. Then she walks her own road.
screen: `A PARTING WITH RESPECT.` · `SHE WAITED FOR AN ORDER OF NUNS.` · `FOREMOST IN HER OWN RIGHT.` · `HER VERSES STAND BESIDE HIS.` · then, large: `HER OWN PATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you're close to, a spouse, a partner, a sibling, a best friend, and a road they walk that isn't yours: a faith, a calling, a craft, a grief. Don't try to join it or fix it. Just picture them on that road, wish them well on it, and stay with the breath.
Bhadda Kapilani. Kassapa's wife, who parted from him at a crossroads, became a nun, and is named foremost among the nuns who remember past lives. Today's word.
Your line: her own path. Side by side, and still her own. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists honor Bhadda Kapilani among the great nuns of the Buddha's time, and her verses are read with the other elder nuns' poems in the Therigatha.

chat.says: Was Bhadda Kapilani famous just for being Mahakassapa's wife?
options: No: the Buddha named her foremost among nuns who remember past lives.
Yes: the texts honor her only as the wife of the great Kassapa.
No: she was famous as the first woman the Buddha ever ordained.
chat.meaning: In her own right she is named foremost among the nuns who remember past lives, and her verses say she too reached the end.

notes: All paraphrased; Mrs. Rhys Davids's Psalms of the Sisters (1909) is public domain, but the writer was not certain of its exact wording.
Crossroads story is commentarial: confirm the reason given (people might think wrongly of them), right for him and left for her. Embellishments (the earth trembling) left out.

Her waiting: the commentary has her stay among other (non-Buddhist) women ascetics until Mahapajapati's order existed; the script says only that she waited and 'lived the homeless life as best she could'. Confirm framing; no length of time given.

Therigatha verses paraphrased: praise of Kassapa as son and heir, knower of former lives and of heaven and hell, ended birth; then 'Bhadda Kapilani' claims the same; both saw the world's peril, went forth, are freed and cooled. Confirm.
'Pubbenivasa' as the gift in AN 1.14: confirm the Pali term used there.
'A few days back' refers to day 739 in this path.
